cls: Arginine vasopressin (AVP) antagonist - dual V1a/V2 receptor antagonist (aquaretic)
quick: 20 mg IV loading over 30 min, then 20 mg/day continuous infusion over 24 h x2-4 days (may titrate to 40 mg/day)
Limited human data; use only if potential benefit justifies fetal risk
Unknown if excreted in milk; not recommended during breastfeeding
Not recommended if CrCl <30 mL/min; little aquaretic benefit and increased risk
Use caution in hepatic impairment; reduced clearance and altered exposure
No specific interaction defined; relevant only to inpatient short-term IV use
Frequent serum sodium, volume and neurologic status; limit rate of sodium rise
summary: Conivaptan (Vaprisol) is an intravenous dual V1a/V2 arginine vasopressin receptor antagonist used in hospitalized patients to raise serum sodium in euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia. By blocking renal V2 receptors it promotes free-water excretion (aquaresis) without major sodium loss. It is given as a 20 mg loading dose over 30 minutes followed by a continuous infusion for a maximum of 4 days, with very frequent monitoring of serum sodium because an overly rapid rise can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome. It is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia and with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors.
indications: Euvolemic hyponatremia (e.g., due to SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, pulmonary disorders) in hospitalized patients
Use is limited to the hospital setting where serum sodium can be monitored frequently

dosage.d: 20 mg IV loading over 30 min, then 20 mg/day infusion
dosage.n: May titrate to 40 mg/day; max 4 days of therapy

dosage.d: Increase continuous infusion from 20 mg/day to 40 mg/day
dosage.n: Only if serum sodium is not rising at the desired rate; total max 4 days
Limited aquaretic effect and increased risk in severe renal impairment

dosage.d: Limit conivaptan to 20 mg/day after the 20 mg loading dose

admin: For intravenous use only; do not give by any other route
Loading dose: infuse 20 mg over 30 minutes
Maintenance: 20 mg given as a continuous infusion over 24 hours (may increase to 40 mg/24 h)
Administer through large veins and rotate the infusion site every 24 hours to limit vascular irritation
Total duration of therapy (loading plus maintenance) should not exceed 4 days
Dilute only as directed (5% dextrose); ensure compatibility before infusing
moa: Conivaptan is a dual antagonist of arginine vasopressin V1a and V2 receptors. Blockade of renal collecting-duct V2 receptors reduces aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption, producing electrolyte-sparing excretion of free water (aquaresis) that raises serum sodium concentration. V1a antagonism affects vascular smooth muscle and the myocardium. The net effect in hyponatremia is increased free-water clearance and correction of low serum sodium.

absolute: Concurrent use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, indinavir)
Known hypersensitivity to conivaptan or any component (including corn or corn products in some formulations)
relative: Severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) - use not recommended
Patients at high risk for too-rapid sodium correction (e.g., chronic, severe hyponatremia, malnutrition, alcoholism, advanced liver disease)
Underlying heart failure when fluid shifts may worsen hemodynamics
monitor: Serum sodium and rate of sodium rise

preg: Limited human data. Animal studies have shown adverse effects. Conivaptan should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: It is not known whether conivaptan is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants, breastfeeding is not recommended during therapy.
renal: Not recommended in patients with creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, in whom there is little expected aquaretic benefit and a greater potential for harm. Use cautiously in lesser degrees of renal impairment and monitor closely.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment; reduced clearance can increase drug exposure. Because conivaptan is metabolized by CYP3A4, hepatic dysfunction may further alter exposure. Consider close monitoring and conservative dosing.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin, ritonavir, indinavir) - CONTRAINDICATED; markedly increase conivaptan exposure
CYP3A4 substrates (e.g., simvastatin, amlodipine, midazolam) - conivaptan inhibits CYP3A4 and can raise their levels
Digoxin - conivaptan increases digoxin exposure; monitor digoxin concentrations
moderate: Moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors - may increase conivaptan levels; limit maintenance dose to 20 mg/day if co-administration is unavoidable
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) - may reduce conivaptan exposure
Other drugs affecting serum sodium or free-water handling (diuretics) - additive effects on sodium
minor: Antihypertensives - possible additive blood pressure or volume effects
interactions.food: Not applicable - administered intravenously; no food interaction
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction has been characterized; relevant mainly to short-term inpatient IV use
interactions.diagnostics: Causes a rise in serum sodium and increased urine output (aquaresis); interpret serial sodium and fluid balance in this context

common: Infusion site reactions (phlebitis, pain, erythema, swelling)
serious: Osmotic demyelination syndrome from too-rapid correction of serum sodium
Hypovolemia and dehydration from excessive aquaresis
rare: Pneumonia / oropharyngeal events reported in trials
emergency: Rapidly rising serum sodium with new neurologic signs (dysarthria, dysphagia, lethargy, quadriparesis) suggesting osmotic demyelination
Severe symptomatic hypotension or hypovolemic shock

monitoring: Serum sodium FREQUENTLY (every few hours during active correction) - do not let it rise too rapidly
Rate of sodium correction: limit the rise (commonly <=8-12 mEq/L per 24 h, slower in high-risk patients)
Neurologic status frequently for signs of osmotic demyelination
Volume/fluid status, blood pressure (including orthostatic), urine output
Infusion site for phlebitis or reactions, rotating site every 24 h
counsel: This medicine is given as an IV infusion in hospital to correct low blood sodium
Your sodium and fluid balance will be checked very often, sometimes every few hours
Tell staff immediately of any new confusion, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, weakness, or unusual drowsiness
Report pain, redness, or swelling at the infusion site
Excess urination and thirst are expected as the medicine removes extra water
pk: Aquaresis (increased free-water excretion) begins within hours of starting infusion
Steady-state plasma concentration reached during continuous infusion (typically within ~12 h)
Effect on serum sodium persists during infusion; monitor for continued sodium rise after stopping
Store ampoules/vials at controlled room temperature; protect as labeled and use prepared infusion promptly per product instructions
pearls: Too-rapid correction of serum sodium can cause irreversible osmotic demyelination syndrome - if sodium rises too fast, discontinue conivaptan and consider administering hypotonic fluid
Strictly limit total therapy to 4 days and reserve for hospitalized patients with frequent sodium monitoring
Contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia - confirm the patient is euvolemic or hypervolemic before use
It is both a strong CYP3A4 substrate and inhibitor: avoid strong CYP3A4 inhibitors entirely and watch CYP3A4 substrates such as statins, midazolam, and digoxin
Rotate the infusion site every 24 hours and use large veins to minimize frequent infusion-site reactions
Not recommended when CrCl is below 30 mL/min because there is little aquaretic benefit
missed: Not applicable in the usual outpatient sense - conivaptan is given as a continuous inpatient IV infusion managed by clinical staff. If an infusion is interrupted, resume per protocol and recheck serum sodium; do not give extra loading doses to 'catch up'.
overdose: No specific antidote. Overdose is expected to cause excessive aquaresis with hypovolemia, hypotension, and a too-rapid rise in serum sodium. Discontinue the infusion, monitor serum sodium and neurologic status closely, and if sodium has risen too fast administer hypotonic fluid (e.g., free water/D5W) and provide supportive care to avoid osmotic demyelination.
